title: Onigiri
subtitle: Japanese rice balls with fillings
excerpt: Onigiri are hand-pressed Japanese rice balls filled with savoury ingredients and wrapped in nori. They are the most portable food in Japanese cuisine and easy to make at home. Makes 8 rice balls.
sourceNotes: Onigiri have been eaten in Japan for over a thousand years. References appear in 11th-century literature. They are the original fast food of Japanese culture and are sold in every convenience store across the country.

recipe.batchNotes: Make a large batch for packed lunches and picnics. Wrap each in cling film and keep at room temperature for up to 6 hours.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Best eaten within a few hours of making. Refrigerating makes the rice hard.

glossaryTerms.definition: Japanese rice balls formed by pressing cooked short-grain rice around a filling with damp hands. Wrapped in nori before eating.
Dried sheets of pressed seaweed used to wrap onigiri and sushi. It adds a savoury, sea-like flavour and holds the rice together for easy eating.

Use short-grain Japanese rice. Long-grain and basmati rice do not have enough starch to hold together when pressed.
Cook the rice and let it cool for 10 minutes until warm but not hot. Stir in sesame seeds if using.
Prepare the filling: flake the salmon and mix with miso paste. Divide the filling into 8 small portions.
Wet your hands with cold water and sprinkle with a small pinch of fine salt. Take about 80g of warm rice and press it into a flat disc in the palm of your hand.

Place a spoonful of filling in the centre. Close the rice around it and shape firmly into a triangle or ball by pressing firmly between both palms. The rice needs to be compact enough to hold together.
Wrap a strip of nori around the base of each onigiri just before serving to keep it crisp. Serve with a small bowl of soy sauce for dipping if you like.

attrs.symptom: Rice ball falls apart when picked up
attrs.cause: Rice was not pressed firmly enough or was too dry
attrs.fix: Press harder when shaping. The rice needs a firm squeeze, not a gentle pat. Wet hands help bind the outer layer.

attrs.cause: Nori was wrapped on while the rice was still hot and steaming
attrs.fix: Wrap nori around each onigiri just before eating, not when making. Keep the nori separate until serving.

attrs.symptom: Rice sticks to hands and tears
attrs.cause: Hands were too dry or too wet
attrs.fix: Wet hands then shake off most of the water. They should be just damp, not dripping. Re-wet between each ball.

content.text: Onigiri are in every Japanese convenience store, sold fresh several times a day. They are the food of train journeys, picnics and school lunchboxes. In Japan the word 'onigiri' is nearly synonymous with the idea of portable food. Japanese families also make them at home to use up leftover rice. Fillings vary endlessly: pickled plum, tuna with mayonnaise, spicy mentaiko roe and soy-marinated salmon are all classics.
